Furthermore, it was discovered that the most advantageous action for each agent in response to an approachable strategy profile can be complex and nonlinear when the distribution of task difficulties is not uniform. A computational method has been established to calculate a cooperative equilibrium through learning within the set of linear policy options. Subsequent experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of this method by generating a cooperative equilibrium that compares favorably with an optimal solution found using dynamic programming. A real-world case study involving a network of sensors detecting poachers showed significant improvements when using this method over current automated decision-making systems. As an alternative to a large strategy space, this method can also be employed to solve cooperative reinforcement learning problems where agents share a environment with partially known statistics. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system where signal and waste light are deeply entangled and coupled, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by at least an order of magnitude in terms of quantum noise performance in the high-frequency range. Moreover, it allows for easier implementation of advanced control schemes, such as optimizing the optical parameters to enhance sensitivity. Using advanced parameters similar to those of the LIGO+ and Einstein Telescope detectors, we demonstrate that this new design can enhance sensitivity to gravitational waves with frequencies over $1\, \mathrm{kHz}$ by at least an order of magnitude. This results in a significant improvement in the mass limit that can be detected, with binary neutron star mergers leading to detection probabilities of $10^{-24}\, \mathrm{erg}^{-1}\, \mathrm{cm}^2$ within reach of future detectors.

Lastly, we employed the linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model to explore a quantum shock wave situation and another with a monatomic gas molecule impinging upon an interacting Bose gas, comparing its outcomes to existing quantum many-body theories.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies. 
This research was presented in a meeting of the American Astronomical Society and is currently undergoing peer review for publication in The Astrophysical Journal.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for learning from a small amount of information obtained directly from newly occurring events. This system leverages a meta-learning approach, combining the advantages of episode-based meta-learning and set-based meta-learning, to enable the model to quickly adapt to newly emerging events with limited information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on newly occurring events, outperforming the current state-of-the-art methods. As an added value, the system is capable of learning to prioritize information that is more relevant to false news detection, leading to further improvement in accuracy. The results obtained on the created benchmarks demonstrate the efficiency of the MetaFEND system in situations where newly occurring events involve additional information such as videos and images. The code and datasets used in this study are available for download at https://github.com/AIforGood META-FEND.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. Furthermore, we show that the Wigner function can be obtained through the optical tomogram for certain non-classical phases of a Schrödinger cat state and a linearized non-degenerate parametric oscillator state. Moreover, we demonstrate the practical application of this approach by verifying the creation of entanglement and sustainable oscillations in a ring resonator filled with a nonlinear medium. 
Theoretical models used include the Dicke state model, the linearized non-degenerate POC model, and the full non-degenerate POC model. The results illustrate the effectiveness of this pattern-recognition state reconstruction method, along with future applications in exploring the behavior of complicated non-linear optical systems.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Moreover, it explores the embedding of spaces with angle functions within Euclidean spaces of various dimensions and presents several related theoretical findings. One of these findings involves the embedding of spaces with angle functions into a line, which serves as a solution to a problem previously addressed by J. Rus. Another finding concerns the equivalence of definitions in regards to spaces with angle functions, which further underscores the article's contributions. The author, M. K. Vesterstein, presents these solutions and findings as part of a broader discussion on the theory of spaces with angle functions, drawing upon existing research by himself and others, including results by A. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system. This theory provides a mechanistic explanation for dust settlement observed in certain areas of protoplanetary disks. It also offers guidance for future studies on dust development and settling models, advising the use of equilibrium equilibrium models or locally reading particle sizes from optical depth data. With this model, we can better understand the formation of ring structures and the settlement of particles seen in the HL Tau disk system. Recreating this system with our model, we predict the formation of a ring structure similar to one observed near 0.05 AU in the HL Tau disk system, along with another at 0.32 AU, consistent with optical depth data. The settlement of particles and the formation of ring structures in protoplanetary disks influence how these systems evolve into planetary systems. With this research, we can improve models of particle development and settling, aiding the creation of realistic protoplanetary disk images and the study of disk evolution. With a more accurate model of dust development and settling behavior, we can investigate the origins of various features seen in ringed protoplanetary disk systems, including the HL Tau disk system, and the formation of planetary systems as a whole.

Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario. This allows us to apply an application of the concavity theory of variance to solve the problem at hand. Our proof also involves a number of other intricate analyses to address potential issues with the boundary and the overall approach. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. Furthermore, we investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. This study provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating the credibility of Bayes factor results, allaying concerns about the stability and reliability of Bayes factors in hypothesis evaluation, and offers utility functions that can be used to make informed decisions based on Bayes factor analysis. This research paves the way for the widespread use of Bayes factor analysis in cognitive science, enabling researchers to compare and contrast competing theories more effectively. The results demonstrate that Bayes factors can accurately identify the preferred hypothesis even when the underlying models are highly complex and variable, and the available data is limited. The findings also show that Bayes factors can consistently distinguish between competing theories that truly differ, as well as identify the true underlying hypothesis generation process when the hypotheses are randomly selected. We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. By integrating these results, we gain a deeper understanding of the underlying principles that underpin the proofs, and more importantly, place the theorems within a broader logical context. Furthermore, we are able to establish a more direct connection between the first incompleteness theorem and the concept of arithmetical definability, which remains undefinable within a formal system as described by Peano arithmetic. Consequently, we can demonstrate that any formal system capable of describing basic mathematical relationships, particularly in a manner analogous to Peano arithmetic, will inevitably be incomplete. This, we believe, provides a more compelling and intuitive justification for the first incompleteness theorem, and its underlying logical foundation, which has been a subject of ongoing debate and interpretation among mathematicians and logicians for nearly a century.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. Furthermore, we discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. The article's final section outlines future directions for research on this topic. 
This work is an enhanced version of three papers that were previously published in the International Journal of Bifurcations and Chaos, the AIMS Mathematics journal, the Journal of Nonlinear Science, and the SIAM Review. The article's key findings offer significant contributions to the theoretical foundation of stability analysis in dynamical systems. It is expected that these discoveries will be utility-focused and lead to the development of efficient stability criteria. Moreover, it is anticipated that these findings will be applicable across a broad spectrum of dynamical systems, including those with polynomial and fractional-order dynamics. The article's primary conclusions are summarized as follows: In planar systems, only linear subspaces can remain invariant when the dynamics is polynomial. In general systems, regardless of the order, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant regions when the dynamics is fractional-order. In fractional-order systems, the size of the invariant linear subspace is limited by the order of the system when the system's order exceeds two. In fractional-order systems, the largest possible invariant linear subspace is a slab in three-dimensional space when the system's order is three or more. In fractional-order systems, the largest possible invariant linear subspace is a paraboloid in four-dimensional space when the system's order is four or more. In fractional-order systems, the largest possible invariant linear subspace is a hyperparaboloid in space of dimension n greater than two when the system's order is greater than n.
